questions.q: In the recurrence T(n) <= aT(n/b) + O(n^d), what does a represent?
choices: The factor by which the problem size shrinks
The exponent of the non-recursive (combination) work
The depth of the recursion tree
questions.explain: a is the coefficient in front of T(.), so it counts how many recursive calls each step makes.

questions.q: In the recurrence T(n) <= aT(n/b) + O(n^d), what does b represent?
choices: The exponent of the combination work
The factor by which the problem size shrinks in each recursive call
The total number of levels in the recursion
questions.explain: b is the divisor inside T(n/b). Each subproblem has size n/b.

questions.q: In the recurrence T(n) <= aT(n/b) + O(n^d), what does d represent?
choices: The exponent of the non-recursive (combination) work
The size of the base case
The factor by which the problem shrinks
questions.explain: d is the exponent inside O(n^d), the work done outside the recursive calls (for example, merging).

questions.q: For T(n) = 3T(n/4) + O(n), what are a, b, and d?
questions.explain: There are 3 recursive calls (a = 3), each on size n/4 (b = 4), and the extra work is O(n) = O(n^1) (d = 1).

questions.q: For T(n) = 2T(n/4) + O(n), what is the value of b?
questions.explain: b is the divisor in T(n/b). Here the subproblems have size n/4, so b = 4. The 2 in front is a, not b.

questions.q: For T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), what is the value of d?
For T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^2), what is b^d?
questions.explain: b = 2 and d = 2, so b^d = 2^2 = 4.

questions.q: To decide which Master Method case applies, which two quantities do you compare?
questions.explain: Always compute b^d first, then compare it with a. Comparing a with b alone is a common mistake.

questions.q: If a < b^d, what is T(n)?
questions.explain: Case 1: a < b^d gives O(n^d). The non-recursive work dominates.

questions.q: If a = b^d, what is T(n)?
questions.explain: Case 2: a = b^d gives O(n^d log n). Don't drop the log n factor.

questions.q: If a > b^d, what is T(n)?
questions.explain: Case 3: a > b^d gives O(n^(log_b a)). The log has base b and argument a. Writing log_a b flips it.

questions.q: In which case does the non-recursive (combination) work dominate the runtime?
choices: None of them; the recursive work always dominates
questions.explain: Case 1: non-recursive work dominates. Case 2: the two are balanced. Case 3: recursive work dominates.

questions.q: In Case 2 (a = b^d), the recursive work and the non-recursive work are balanced.
questions.explain: Neither dominates in Case 2, which is why the runtime picks up a log n factor: O(n^d log n).

questions.q: In Case 3 (a > b^d), the value of d appears in the final runtime.
questions.explain: Case 3 gives O(n^(log_b a)), which depends only on a and b. d is used only to decide which case applies.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the Master Method are correct?
choices: In Case 3, the recursive subproblems dominate the runtime.
Case 2's runtime is O(n^d), the same as Case 1.
You should compute b^d before comparing it with a.
In Case 3, the exponent is log_a b.
In Case 1, the runtime is determined by the combination work O(n^d).
questions.explain: Case 2 is O(n^d log n), not O(n^d). The Case 3 exponent is log_b a, not log_a b.

questions.q: The Rate of Subproblem Proliferation (RSP) corresponds to which quantity in T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d)?
questions.explain: RSP is a, the number of new subproblems each call creates. For example, 8T(n/2) creates 8 calls at each step.

questions.q: The Rate of Work Shrinkage (RSW) corresponds to which quantity in T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d)?
questions.explain: RSW is b^d, which measures how much the work per subproblem shrinks.

questions.q: If RSP > RSW, which case applies and what is the runtime?
questions.explain: RSP > RSW means a > b^d. Subproblems multiply faster than the work shrinks, so it is Case 3: O(n^(log_b a)).

questions.q: When RSP < RSW, the work shrinks faster than the subproblems multiply, and the runtime is O(n^d).
questions.explain: RSP < RSW means a < b^d, which is Case 1: O(n^d).

questions.q: If RSP = RSW, what is the runtime?
questions.explain: RSP = RSW means a = b^d. The two balance, which is Case 2: O(n^d log n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).
questions.explain: a = 2, b = 2, d = 1, so b^d = 2. a = b^d gives Case 2: O(n^1 log n) = O(n log n). This is Merge Sort.

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 3T(n/4) + O(n).
questions.explain: a = 3, b = 4, d = 1, so b^d = 4. 3 < 4 gives Case 1: O(n^d) = O(n).

questions.q: Which Master Method case applies to T(n) = 2T(n/4) + O(n)? (Answer with the case number.)
questions.explain: a = 2, b^d = 4^1 = 4. 2 < 4, so it is Case 1, giving O(n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + O(n^2).
choices: O(n^(log_3 9)) = O(n^2), with no log factor
questions.explain: a = 9, b = 3, d = 2, so b^d = 3^2 = 9. a = b^d gives Case 2: O(n^2 log n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n).
questions.explain: a = 3, b = 2, d = 1, so b^d = 2. 3 > 2 gives Case 3: O(n^(log_2 3)), about O(n^1.585).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n^2).
questions.explain: a = 2, b = 2, d = 2, so b^d = 4. 2 < 4 gives Case 1: O(n^d) = O(n^2).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).
questions.explain: a = 1, b = 2, d = 0 (since O(1) = O(n^0)), so b^d = 2^0 = 1. a = b^d gives Case 2: O(n^0 log n) = O(log n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 16T(n/4) + O(n^2).
questions.explain: a = 16, b = 4, d = 2, so b^d = 4^2 = 16. a = b^d gives Case 2: O(n^2 log n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1).
Which of these recurrences fall into Case 3 (a > b^d)?
A student says T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n^2) is Case 3 because 4 > 2. What is the correct analysis?
choices: The student is right: Case 3, O(n^2)
The student compared a with b instead of b^d. b^d = 4 = a, so it is Case 2: O(n^2 log n)
b^d = 4 > a is false, so it is Case 1: O(n^2)
The Master Method does not apply because d = 2
questions.explain: b^d = 2^2 = 4, which equals a = 4. That is Case 2, giving O(n^2 log n).

questions.q: Use the Master Method: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^3).
choices: O(n^(log_2 8)) = O(n^3), with no log factor
questions.explain: a = 8, b = 2, d = 3, so b^d = 2^3 = 8. a = b^d gives Case 2: O(n^3 log n).

questions.q: How many recursive matrix multiplications does standard divide-and-conquer matrix multiplication (splitting each matrix into four blocks) require?
questions.explain: XY = [[AE + BG, AF + BH], [CE + DG, CF + DH]] uses 8 products: AE, BG, AF, BH, CE, DG, CF, DH.

questions.q: Standard divide-and-conquer matrix multiplication has T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^2). What is its runtime?
How many recursive matrix multiplications does Strassen's method use?
questions.explain: Strassen reduces the recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, giving T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2).

questions.q: Strassen's method runs in O(n^(log_2 7)). To three decimal places, what is log_2 7?
questions.explain: log_2 7 is about 2.807, so Strassen runs in about O(n^2.807).

questions.q: Why does Strassen's method beat the standard O(n^3) divide-and-conquer matrix multiplication?
choices: It reduces the combination work from O(n^2) to O(n)
It splits the matrices into more blocks, which increases b
It changes the recurrence from Case 3 to Case 2
It reduces the recursive calls from 8 to 7, which lowers the Case 3 exponent log_b a from 3 to about 2.807
questions.explain: Both are Case 3, where the runtime is O(n^(log_b a)). Lowering a from 8 to 7 lowers the exponent directly: log_2 8 = 3, log_2 7 is about 2.807.

questions.q: Splitting two n-digit integers as X = 10^(n/2)a + b and Y = 10^(n/2)c + d and computing XY = 10^n(ac) + 10^(n/2)(ad + bc) + bd gives which recurrence and runtime?
questions.explain: Four recursive products (ac, ad, bc, bd) on n/2-digit numbers plus O(n) extra work. a = 4, b^d = 2^1 = 2, 4 > 2 gives Case 3: O(n^(log_2 4)) = O(n^2).

questions.q: In the split integer multiplication X = 10^(n/2)a + b, Y = 10^(n/2)c + d, which products must be computed recursively to get XY = 10^n(ac) + 10^(n/2)(ad + bc) + bd?
questions.explain: The expansion needs ac, ad, bc, and bd: four recursive products.

questions.q: In the integer multiplication split X = 10^(n/2)a + b, Y = 10^(n/2)c + d, the letters a and b are the same as the Master Method parameters a and b.
questions.explain: Here a, b, c, d are the digit halves of the numbers. The Master Method parameters for this algorithm are a = 4 (recursive calls), b = 2, d = 1.

questions.q: Which of these algorithms falls into Master Method Case 2?
choices: Recursive integer multiplication with four recursive products
questions.explain: Merge Sort: 2T(n/2) + O(n), a = 2 = 2^1 = b^d, so Case 2, O(n log n). The other three are all Case 3.
